title: How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury
authors: Soligard T, Schwellnus M, Alonso JM, Bahr R, Clarsen B, Dijkstra HP, et al.
population: Elite and competitive athletes across sports (expert group, 18 authors)
findings: Emerging evidence indicates poor load management is a major risk factor for injury.
Load is defined broadly: rapid changes in training and competition load, competition calendar congestion, psychological load and travel.
The statement gives guidelines for prescription of training and competition load and for monitoring of training, competition and psychological load, athlete well-being and injury.
Load is defined broadly (rapid changes in training and competition load, calendar congestion, psychological load, travel).

The statement gives guidelines for prescription of training and competition load and for monitoring of training, competition and psychological load, athlete well-being and injury, and identifies research priorities.
Load is defined broadly to include rapid changes in training and competition load, calendar congestion, psychological load and travel.
The statement gives guidelines for prescribing and for monitoring training load, athlete well-being and injury.
limitations: Abstract is qualitative and provides no numeric thresholds. Multi-sport elite focus; its ACWR guidance is the target of later critiques (Impellizzeri 2020, Wang 2020).
implications: Supports monitoring load changes alongside well-being and non-training stress (sleep, illness, travel) as modifiers of risk; a well-being input to adaptive rules is reasonable but unquantified.
No numeric parameter can be taken from this paper.
Supports pairing a monitored, gradual load ramp with well-being monitoring rather than relying on a single threshold.
Provides authority for including psychological and life-load inputs (for example, travel or illness) as reasons to reduce load; no numeric parameters follow from it.
Support a gradual-progression rule and monitoring of rapid load changes, without a specific number.
Pair any ratio guard (see Toresdahl 2023) with athlete-reported well-being and let the athlete adjust the plan.

verification.notes: Crossref: BJSM 50:1030-1041 (Aug 2016). Abstract matched. Grade set to B (not A) because content is qualitative and the ACWR parts were later criticised.
